title: Comelec must stop acting abusively, whimsically
keywords: six million ballots discarded P22 each
primary_topics: Author's third public chastisement of the Comelec and its chair George Erwin Garcia (GEG) for repeated 'grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction' (GAD) -- defining GAD as discretion that is 'not only abusive, but gravely abusive, whimsical, arbitrary, capricious, and actuated by personal bias or hostility or ill will'

Catalogue of recent SC GAD findings against the Comelec: Smartmatic v. Comelec (15-0); De Guzman-Lara v. Comelec (13-0-2; 24-hours-in-a-day computation); Macalintal v. Comelec (party-list ex-parte TRO); the Cortes, Rosal, Rama disqualification TROs (Oct 28, 2024 column); Ollesca v. Comelec (nuisance-candidate void); Jan 14 and Jan 17 2025 TRO barrage in 8 more cases

Doctrinal anchor on nuisance candidates: under Omnibus Election Code Section 69, nuisance candidates have 'no bona fide intention to run' and merely put the election process in mockery or disrepute or cause voter confusion; lack of financial capacity is not by itself a ground because it imposes an unconstitutional property qualification; burden of proof lies with the alleger, not the candidate

Operational consequence: for the first time in its history, the Comelec stopped the ongoing printing of ballots and discarded about 6 million of them (costing P22 each) to print new ones including the petitioners' names

Author's diagnostic conclusion: the Comelec's repeated failures to observe basic constitutional rights to due process and equal protection shame and ruin its vaunted competence and independence -- and especially the reputation of its chair GEG, an 'eminent election lawyer' known for integrity and trustworthiness
sub_topics: Author's two prior columns referenced: 'Quo vadis, George Erwin Garcia?' (Oct 14, 2024) and 'Comelec, GEG knocked but not yet out' (Oct 28, 2024)
Definition of GAD: discretion not only abusive but 'gravely abusive, whimsical, arbitrary, capricious, and actuated by personal bias or hostility or ill will'

Smartmatic v. Comelec (April 16, 2024, per J. Jose Midas P. Marquez, en banc, 15-0): SC lambasted Comelec for barring Smartmatic from 'participating in any public bidding for elections' due merely to information from US about ongoing criminal investigation of former chair Andres Bautista -- violation of due process
De Guzman-Lara v. Comelec (Aug 6, 2024, per J. Jhosep Y. Lopez, en banc, 13-0-2): SC called out Comelec for failing to compute that a day is composed of 24 hours

Macalintal v. Comelec: en banc ex-parte TRO stopping Comelec from allowing public appointive officials accepting party-list nominations from staying in office for ~2 months until campaign-period start

Cortes, Rosal, Rama TROs (Oct 28, 2024 column): SC en banc TROs stopping Comelec from disqualifying Mandaue Mayor Jonas Cortes, former Albay governor Noel Rosal, and Cebu Mayor Michael Rama for the 2025 elections because the Ombudsman dismissal orders have not attained finality -- 'elementary it is that a decision that has not become final is not a source of disqualifications or adverse conclusions'
Jan 14, 2025 TRO barrage in 5 cases: Mustapha, Savellano, Balintay, Erice, Ritualo v. Comelec
Jan 17, 2025 TRO barrage in 3 more cases: David, Oñate, Sta. Ana v. Comelec -- all arbitrarily declared 'nuisance candidates'

Ollesca v. Comelec (July 30, 2024, per Senior Associate Justice Marvic MVF Leonen, en banc, 13-0-2, released Jan 14, 2025): voided for GAD a Comelec resolution declaring petitioner a nuisance candidate for president in 2022 elections; case decided despite mootness to guide Comelec
Omnibus Election Code Section 69 definition: nuisance candidates have no bona fide intention to run; merely put process in mockery or disrepute or cause voter confusion
Comelec's basis for the Ollesca declaration: petitioner's failure to show financial capacity to 'sustain a decent and viable campaign on his own'

SC's two-part rebuttal: (1) lack of financial capacity is not a ground because it imposes a property qualification barred by the Constitution; (2) burden of proof belongs to the alleger, not the candidate; Comelec cannot rely on mere speculation that petitioner as 'an unknown aspirant' lacked the capacity
Comelec's TRO-obedient action: for the first time in history, stopped ongoing ballot printing and discarded ~6 million ballots (costing P22 each) to print new ones including the petitioners' names
More similar cases awaiting Court action noted

Author's pointed observation: 'I do not remember any Comelec that has committed as many gravely abusive acts again and again and again on practically the same ground' -- failure to observe due process and equal protection
Author's appeal to GEG personally: heretofore enjoyed enviable reputation for integrity and trustworthiness; multiple GADs shame and ruin Comelec's vaunted competence and independence

stances.claim: The Comelec under GEG has committed an unprecedented number of GADs — 'gravely abusive, whimsical, arbitrary, capricious, and actuated by personal bias or hostility or ill will' — repeatedly on the same ground: failure to observe due process and equal protection.
stances.rhetorical_move: third-time-warning escalation with named-chair public accountability
stances.evidence: Catalogue of SC rulings: Smartmatic, De Guzman-Lara, Macalintal, Cortes/Rosal/Rama, Mustapha/Savellano/Balintay/Erice/Ritualo, David/Oñate/Sta. Ana, Ollesca

stances.claim: Smartmatic exemplifies the basic error: Comelec banned a vendor from public bidding 'due merely to information from the United States regarding an ongoing criminal investigation of former Comelec chair Andres Bautista' — without observing due process even 'first year law students' know is required.
stances.evidence: Smartmatic v. Comelec (15-0 en banc); due-process doctrine

stances.claim: Lack of financial capacity, by itself, is not a ground for nuisance-candidate disqualification — it imposes a property qualification that is barred by the Constitution; the burden of proof belongs to the party alleging the fact (the Comelec), not the candidate; the Comelec cannot rely on mere speculation that an unknown aspirant lacks the capacity to wage a nationwide campaign.
stances.evidence: Omnibus Election Code Section 69; constitutional bar on property qualifications; SC ruling in Ollesca

stances.claim: The Comelec's TRO-obedient action — stopping ballot printing for the first time in its history and discarding about 6 million ballots at P22 each — is a measurable national cost of the repeated GADs, with more similar cases pending.
stances.evidence: 6M ballots × P22 = ~P132M; Comelec's own operational disclosure

stances.claim: The repeated GADs 'shame and ruin the vaunted competence and independence of the Comelec especially of its chair, GEG, who heretofore had enjoyed an enviable reputation for integrity and trustworthiness' — the institution and its chair must learn lessons and avoid embarrassing rebukes from the Court and the public.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-reputation appeal anchored on prior credibility
stances.evidence: Author's prior characterization of GEG as 'eminent election lawyer'; pattern of repeated rulings

notable_anecdotes: The 15-0 unanimous SC vote in Smartmatic v. Comelec — used to underscore that even one justice's dissent did not survive the Comelec's basic due-process failure.
De Guzman-Lara v. Comelec calling out the Comelec for failing to compute that 'a day is composed of 24 hours' — the column's most-quoted absurdity-of-error moment.
The Jan 14 and Jan 17 2025 TRO barrages in 8 different cases (5 + 3) — surfaced as evidence of a pattern, not an isolated incident.

The Ollesca case decided despite mootness (the 2022 presidential elections already over) 'to guide the Comelec from repeating its arbitrary actions' — and the irony that the Comelec repeated the same gravely-abusive acts in the three David/Oñate/Sta. Ana cases anyway.
Comelec stopping ballot printing 'for the first time in its history' and discarding ~6 million ballots at P22 each — used as the column's concrete public-cost anchor.

Author's named-chair public-accountability move: GEG known as 'an eminent election lawyer' with 'enviable reputation for integrity and trustworthiness' — set up so the institutional shaming has personal weight.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers his third public chastisement of the Commission on Elections and its chair George Erwin Garcia (GEG) -- whom he has known as 'an eminent election lawyer' -- for repeatedly committing 'grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction' (GAD), defined as discretion that is 'not only abusive, but gravely abusive, whimsical, arbitrary, capricious, and actuated by personal bias or hostility or ill will.' He cross-references his Oct 14, 2024 column ('Quo vadis, George Erwin Garcia?') noting that the SC, in Smartmatic v. Comelec (April 16, 2024, per J. Jose Midas P. Marquez, en banc, 15-0), lambasted the Commission for barring Smartmatic from public bidding 'due merely to information from the United States regarding an ongoing criminal investigation of former Comelec chair Andres Bautista' -- when even first-year law students know due process must be observed; De Guzman-Lara v. Comelec (Aug 6, 2024, per J. Jhosep Y. Lopez, en banc, 13-0-2) called out the Comelec for failing to compute that a day is composed of 24 hours; Macalintal v. Comelec featured an en banc ex-parte TRO stopping the Comelec from allowing public appointive officials accepting party-list nominations from staying in office for about two months until the campaign period begins. His Oct 28, 2024 column ('Comelec, GEG knocked but not yet out') flagged TROs stopping the Comelec from disqualifying Mandaue City Mayor Jonas C. Cortes, former Albay governor Noel E. Rosal, and Cebu City Mayor Michael L. Rama from the 2025 elections because the Ombudsman dismissal orders had not attained finality -- 'elementary it is that a decision that has not become final is not a source of disqualifications or adverse conclusions.' On Jan 14, 2025, the SC issued a fresh TRO barrage in five cases (Mustapha, Savellano, Balintay, Erice, Ritualo v. Comelec), followed Jan 17 by three more (David, Oñate, Sta. Ana v. Comelec) -- all involving petitioners arbitrarily declared 'nuisance candidates.' Earlier, Ollesca v. Comelec (July 30, 2024, per Senior Associate Justice Marvic MVF Leonen, en banc, 13-0-2, released Jan 14, 2025) voided a Comelec resolution declaring the petitioner a nuisance candidate for president in 2022 -- decided despite mootness 'to guide the Comelec from repeating its arbitrary actions,' which the Commission did anyway. Under Omnibus Election Code Section 69, nuisance candidates have 'no bona fide intention to run' and merely put the election process in mockery or disrepute or cause voter confusion. The Comelec had based its declaration on the petitioner's failure to show financial capacity to 'sustain a decent and viable campaign on his own'; the Court held that (1) lack of financial capacity by itself is not a ground because it imposes an unconstitutional property qualification, and (2) the burden of proof belongs to the party alleging the fact (the Comelec), not the candidate, and the Comelec cannot rely on mere speculation that an unknown aspirant lacks campaign capacity. In obedience to the TROs, the Comelec -- for the first time in its history -- stopped the ongoing printing of ballots and discarded about 6 million of them (at P22 each) to print new ones including the names of the petitioners arbitrarily excluded; more similar cases are pending. Author concludes that he does not 'remember any Comelec that has committed as many gravely abusive acts again and again and again on practically the same ground -- the failure to observe the very basic constitutional rights to due process and equal protection of the laws,' and that these 'shame and ruin the vaunted competence and independence of the Comelec especially of its chair, GEG, who heretofore had enjoyed an enviable reputation for integrity and trustworthiness.' The Comelec 'must stop its gravely abusive, arbitrary, whimsical, and capricious actions and attend to its mandate to be fair, objective, and judicious in exercising its quasi-judicial functions. It must learn lessons and avoid embarrassing rebukes from the Court and the public.'
